title: COP31 failed to deliver. How climate negotiations can move forward from here
content_html:
By Sameer Kwatra

Climate change is no longer a forecast. This year has brought catastrophic floods in Nepal that left thousands dead or missing, severe drought pushing 6.5 million people into acute hunger in Somalia, extreme heat across South Asia, a heat dome over North America, wildfires across Canada and a European summer where extreme heat claimed more than 50,000 lives.

Advertisement

Climate change is powerful and persistent; no country is immune, and the cost is not borne equally. And yet, even as the planet is smoldering, 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, demonstrated that the negotiations remain frozen in time. Despite being the longest COP to date, the process could not yield any agreement on either fossil fuels or finance.

To be fair, the multilateral COP framework has helped bend the curve on carbon emissions. Three decades ago, the world was hurtling toward 4 degrees Celsius of warming by the end of this century; today, projections point to roughly 2.8 degrees. Global diplomacy has also dragged climate change from the footnotes of national agendas into the spotlight.

Yet from COP1 in Berlin to COP31 in Antalya, the same fundamental questions remain unanswered: who pays and how much, who acts and how much?

Modest expectations

Advertisement

Expectations heading into Antalya were modest from the start. Framed as a technical summit focused on implementation rather than historic breakthroughs, COP31 took place in a world riven by geopolitical tensions, and the final COP31 decision mirrors that reality. The shortfalls are clearest on three fronts: fossil fuels, electrification and adaptation finance.

Even as the text admits for the first time that the world will likely overshoot the 1.5°C warming limit, (until the last push) it refused to name fossil fuels, the primary culprit. Earlier versions echoed the hard-won COP28 pledge to move away from fossil fuels and floated transition roadmaps; the failed final version retreated into vague language about shifting toward low-emissions, paired with contested references to carbon capture and removal.

Also Read | COP31: Why climate summits still matter, even as the world misses its targets

Add to that, the Turkish presidency’s flagship push for 35% electrification by 2035 raised many questions about about what would power the electrification, will it lead to electrifying existing energy use or be subsumed in large growth of data centers, and finally who would pay for the immense investment needed for countries to electrify.

The missing ingredient is political will, not money. Wealthy nations cite constrained public budgets to justify stalling on climate finance, yet governments continue to direct hundreds of billions of dollars into fossil fuel subsidies, and risk expanding them in 2026 to cushion energy price spikes. Meanwhile, seven of the world’s largest oil and gas companies pocketed $150 billion in profits during the first nine months of the year.

A new playbook

Climate diplomacy needs a new playbook. Two practical shifts can get negotiations moving again: an integrated bargain that ties action to payment, and climate “minilateralism” in smaller coalitions.

The first is an integrated bargain. Rather than negotiating emissions cuts, finance for mitigation and adaptation, and technology in separate rooms, negotiators should move action, payment, and technology together. That comes down to four straightforward steps:

  1. Each country defines what needs to be done and what it actually costs;
  2. Wealthy nations agree on realistic contributions;
  3. Predictable funding and technology access are linked directly to measurable actions by developing nations;
  4. And timelines are staggered based on what each country can reasonably handle.

The second shift is climate “minilateralism”, an approach that has been discussed in various forms for the last several years. Think of this as “climate breakout rooms” where participants hash out thorny issues outside of the COP arena but report back to the full gathering. This would require smaller groupings such as the G20, BRICS and the Quad putting climate on their permanent agendas.

Also Read | Before COPs: The turning point in climate talks

By hammering out practical deals on clean technology, resilient infrastructure, and early warning systems in smaller rooms, these coalitions can bring ready-made solutions back to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, so that COP shifts from an arena for endless positional posturing into a place where deals are actually finalised. Crucially, the COP process must stay inclusive to ensure that the most at-risk blocs, such as the Least Developed Countries and the Alliance of Small Island States, have a direct voice in shaping the outcomes.

Neither idea replaces the UN framework but gives it the engine it has been missing. Negotiators can soften draft texts and argue over baselines, but communities from Nepal to Europe cannot negotiate a delay with the next flood, drought or heatwave. Global warming is now a global warning.

Sameer Kwatra is the Senior Director, India at the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), a US-based environmental non-profit organisation

title: Tata Steel’s APL Apollo deal: Why investors are worried about the Rs 28,000-crore bet
content_html:

Tata Steel on Wednesday (November 25) said it was reviewing the structure of its proposed Rs 28,000-crore deal with APL Apollo Tubes, following investor backlash. The concerns centre on the deal’s valuation, how it will be financed, the risk of dilution for shareholders and commercial arrangements involving a promoter-linked entity.

After a sharp fall of over 21% on Monday, APL Apollo shares have fallen another 11.4% on Wednesday. Tata Steel’s shares also declined 2.54%, after the 8% fall on Monday, in a strong market following concerns over the cost of the acquisition and how the company intends to fund it.

While the strategic rationale is clear, the financial implications for shareholders, who were flummoxed by the two-leg transaction, remain less so. There may be a case for expansion, but the price it pays and the manner in which it finances the transaction ultimately determine whether shareholders benefit.

Why is the market uneasy?

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

On Sunday, Tata Steel announced plans to sell its entire steel tubes business and its wholly owned subsidiary, Tata Steel Colors Pvt Ltd, to APL Apollo Tubes for a combined consideration of Rs 28,000 crore. A day later, Tata Steel said it will acquire a 26.6% stake in APL Apollo Tubes from its promoters – Sanjay Gupta and family – for Rs 15,510 crore and make an open offer for an additional 26 per cent stake.

Effectively, APL Apollo would borrow Rs 28,000 crore to buy two Tata businesses and Tata Steel, in turn, would use that money to buy out APL Apollo’s Guptas. Investors are debating whether minority shareholders will approve the transfer of two business units as promoters – mostly Tata Sons – hold only 32.94% in Tata Sons.

Even as Tata Steel MD TV Narendran on Wednesday indicated that it will review the acquisition structure, the market is apparently worried about the valuation of the transaction, financing structure and the impact on minority shareholders.

Also in Explained | Sensex surges 2,000 points intraday: Why is the stock market rallying?

The approximately Rs 28,000-crore valuation attributed to the tubes and colour-coated businesses has drawn scrutiny, particularly in comparison with the historical net block of the assets being transferred. Questions have also surfaced over the valuation of Tata Steel Colors following the buyout of its joint venture partner, BlueScope.

Story continues below this ad

In a conference call on Monday, Tata Steel CFO Koushik Chatterjee has defended the valuation, arguing that historical asset values do not adequately capture the growth prospects, distribution advantages and operational synergies of the businesses. While businesses are valued on their future cash flows rather than their asset costs, the assumptions underpinning those projections matter.

“Investors need greater clarity on expected revenue growth, operating margins, capital expenditure and the return on invested capital,” said an investment analyst. “The valuation will ultimately have to be justified through earnings and cash flows. Projected synergies, however attractive on paper, cannot be treated as realised returns.”

Investors are also weighing execution risks, leverage, integration challenges and the time required for the acquisition to contribute meaningfully to earnings.

Financing the deal, risk of dilution

The financing structure is a source of concern for investors. Of the approximately Rs 28,000-crore consideration, around Rs 10,000 crore is expected to remain as external debt, with the balance to be addressed through equity or other capitalisation instruments. The management has indicated that APL Apollo’s net debt-to-EBITDA ratio is expected to decline to approximately 2.5 times within 12 months of closing. The route to achieving this target, however, will be important for shareholders.

Story continues below this ad
Also Read | When bosses must pay back: How malus and clawback provisions work — and don’t work — in India

“Fresh equity issuance at an unfavourable valuation could dilute existing shareholders, while higher debt could increase interest costs and constrain cash flows. The financing structure is therefore central to the transaction, not merely a technical detail to be settled after the acquisition,” said a fund manager tracking the deal.

Chatterjee has said the instruments will be structured fairly and will not prejudice existing shareholders. Tata Steel has also indicated that it will not vote on the relevant resolution at APL Apollo’s shareholder meeting, leaving continuing shareholders to decide on the material transaction. The assurances will need to be backed by transparent terms, including the pricing and nature of the instruments and their implications for existing shareholders, analysts assert.

Narendran said APL Apollo’s established brand, distribution network and customer relationships, built over 15-20 years, would be difficult and time-consuming for Tata Steel to replicate organically. While the acquisition offers faster market access and complements Tata Steel’s downstream business, the key question is whether the premium paid will generate adequate returns or erode shareholder value if expected synergies take longer to materialise.

SG Group arrangement raises governance questions

The proposed exclusive contract-manufacturing arrangement with SG Tech Engineering, a private entity associated with APL Apollo’s promoter group, adds another dimension to the transaction. Contract manufacturing can help companies expand without committing substantial capital to new facilities.

Story continues below this ad

Narendran has argued that the arrangement will allow Tata Steel to grow its colour-coated products business without investing directly in additional manufacturing capacity.

However, a commercial arrangement involving a promoter-linked entity warrants closer scrutiny, particularly when shareholders are evaluating a transaction of this scale. Pricing, operating costs, capital expenditure, capacity commitments, contractual duration and the allocation of risks need to be clearly disclosed. Investors must be able to assess whether the arrangement is commercially beneficial to the listed entity.

Also Read | Rooftop solar rules: Why the Centre wants users to install storage, pay for excess power

Management has said that transactions between Tata Steel and APL Apollo will be conducted at market rates and on an arm’s-length basis.

For Tata Steel shareholders, the acquisition raises the question of whether the capital committed to the transaction could generate better returns through strengthening existing operations, reducing debt or pursuing organic expansion. APL Apollo’s continuing public shareholders, meanwhile, will have to assess whether the proposed recapitalisation and associated commercial arrangements distribute risks and rewards fairly.

title: COP31 ends without climate deal. Why, and what does that mean for India?
content_html:
Activists participate in a demonstration holding signs that say "shame" and "failure" at the COP31 U.N. Climate Summit, Nov. 20, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. (AP Photo/Khalil Hamra, File)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) expects 2026 to rank amongst the four warmest years on record, with a very strong El Niño building into 2027. Europe’s deadly summer heat, the flash floods in Nepal and India’s own summer season tested public systems everywhere this year. The war in Iran led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, driving up the price of oil, gas and fertiliser.

It is in this context that COP31 in Antalya closed on November 22 without adopting its cover decision – the proposed Antalya Pact, which would have set out a common political direction for global climate action, including on emissions reduction, the energy transition and climate finance. It is the first UN climate summit since Copenhagen in 2009 to end without an overarching political outcome.

A cover decision is not legally binding but serves as an important political signal. It is where the conference says, in a single voice, what the world agrees on and where it goes next. Almost every conference of recent years has produced one, from Glasgow’s “phase-down” of coal in 2021 to Dubai’s call to transition away from fossil fuels in 2023, and even Belém’s promise to triple adaptation finance in 2025.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

This year, the cover decision mattered more than usual. With the world falling miserably short on emissions cuts to keep the 1.5℃ target in sight, this COP was the one venue where all countries could renew their climate ambitions to keep the Paris Agreement’s targets alive.

I’m deeply disappointed that #COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome.

I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands.

But this setback does not change the facts.

There may be no consensus in the negotiating room, but there is no ambiguity in the science.

The take-home message from COP31 is clear:

The world must do much more to confront the climate crisis.

And it must do it now.

https://t.co/j05tHQA8AM

— António Guterres (@antonioguterres) November 22, 2026

The absence of a cover decision also sets a concerning precedent. Even relatively ‘weaker’ COPs still produced a cover text. This helps restore confidence in the multilateral process to address problems of global nature such as climate change. After the failed 2009 Copenhagen conference, it took six years of rebuilding trust to reach the Paris Agreement. Cover decisions, though not binding, also signal the direction of travel to everyone outside the room, such as finance ministries, investors and regulators.

What were the pressure points that led to a no-deal?

The breaking point was the cause of the crisis itself. More than 130 countries backed a call to move away from fossil fuels during the talks. Yet the final draft did not name coal, oil or gas, and referred only to the Dubai outcome, which had called for transitioning away from fossil fuels.

Instead, the draft offered a global aspiration to scale carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) to gigatonne levels by 2035, and a goal of raising the share of electricity in final energy use to 35% by 2035. While carbon removal remains an important area of research, it cannot on its own keep the 1.5°C target under the Paris Agreement alive. Reducing greenhouse gas emissions thus becomes non-negotiable.

Story continues below this ad
Also in Explained | COP31: Why climate summits still matter, even as the world misses its targets

For some negotiators, including those representing the EU and countries such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, a text that could not name fossil fuels but could champion carbon capture read as a retreat from Dubai. For Saudi Arabia, speaking for the Arab states, however, carbon capture was the point: it lets producers cut emissions without cutting output. Russia also objected, and for now there is no formal mitigation process at all.

Yet there is hope. Outside COP31, Brazil handed over its voluntary roadmap for transitioning away from fossil fuels, and Denmark, Spain and Portugal announced national plans.

Money, or a lack thereof, was also a major reason for this failure. Disagreements over new, quantified climate finance pledges added fuel to the fire. Developing countries said wealthier nations must provide adequate financial assistance and that developing countries shouldn’t be expected to make ambitious commitments without it. Wealthier, developed countries made no new collective financial commitments. Their announcements were selective and leaned on loans and private capital. For now, the finance work programme has survived as a process but without new money behind it.

Where did India stand, and what did it secure?

India came to Antalya with a familiar brief. Its third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), submitted in April 2026, commits to a 47% cut in emissions intensity from 2005 levels and a share of about 60% for non-fossil sources in installed power capacity by 2035. It had already crossed the 50% threshold for non-fossil capacity, five years ahead of its 2030 target. Working with BASIC (Brazil, South Africa, India, China) and the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs), India pressed for public finance under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement. It wanted mitigation talks to stay bottom-up, country-driven, facilitative and non-punitive, and it opposed unilateral measures such as the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).

Story continues below this ad

While India remained dissatisfied with the dilution of the text on developed countries’ historical responsibility, it was successful in getting its key points into the draft text: a) developed countries’ Article 9.1 obligations were recalled; and b) equity and common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) were placed at the heart of implementation.

Also Read | What COP31 collapse means for India – and the future of climate change policy

Interestingly, India also recognised the need for reducing anthropogenic methane emissions and the near-term climate benefits of reducing such short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs). This marks a welcome shift from its previous position, with India finally recognising the near-term climate benefits of reducing methane emissions while maintaining its stand on food security.

What does the lack of a unified vision mean for climate policy, and for India?

The easy reading is that Antalya failed. The harder one is that it failed honestly. A text that could not name fossil fuels, wrote a gigatonne aspiration for carbon capture into a UN decision and deleted the only number on adaptation finance would not have been a compromise. It would have been a step back dressed as consensus. No deal was better than that deal.

The cost of the stalemate is still real, and it falls on trust. The regime now runs on two currencies, ambition and money, and each camp holds one hostage to the other. Developed countries want fossil-fuel language without new finance. Producers want carbon capture without fossil-fuel language. Developing countries want finance before ambition. Under the consensus rule, everyone holds a veto and no one holds the pen.

Story continues below this ad

Subscribe

The deeper risk is fragmentation. When parties to the UNFCCC cannot agree, rules get written elsewhere: in coalitions of the willing on fossil fuels, in voluntary pledges and in trade policy such as CBAM. These are spaces where CBDR carries little weight. For India, a weak multilateral process is not a win. It is the loss of the one forum where equity is the law of the room. The ICJ’s advisory opinion last year gave legal weight to arguments India has long made, but that weight is useful only in a forum that still works.

So, India must do two things at once. It must keep pressing for public finance and opposing unilateral trade measures at COP32 in Addis Ababa and through the second global stocktake that concludes in 2028. And it must move faster where no consensus text is needed: cutting methane emissions from waste and fossil fuels, phasing down HFCs under the Kigali Amendment, and reducing black carbon emissions. Cutting these super-pollutants is the quickest way to shave near-term warming. A summit without a deal is a setback. A decade without action would be a far bigger one.

What were the pressure points that led to a no-deal?
The breaking point was the cause of the crisis itself. More than 130 countries backed a call to move away from fossil fuels during the talks. Yet the final draft did not name coal, oil or gas, and referred only to the Dubai outcome, which had called for transitioning away from fossil fuels.
Instead, the draft offered a global aspiration to scale carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) to gigatonne levels by 2035, and a goal of raising the share of electricity in final energy use to 35% by 2035. COP31: Why climate summits still matter, even as the world misses its targets
For some negotiators, including those representing the EU and countries such as Panama and the Marshall Islands, a text that could not name fossil fuels but could champion carbon capture read as a retreat from Dubai. Russia also objected, and for now there is no formal mitigation process at all.

Money, or a lack thereof, was also a major reason for this failure. Disagreements over new, quantified climate finance pledges added fuel to the fire. Developing countries said wealthier nations must provide adequate financial assistance and that developing countries shouldn’t be expected to make ambitious commitments without it. Wealthier, developed countries made no new collective financial commitments. Their announcements were selective and leaned on loans and private capital. For now, the finance work programme has survived as a process but without new money behind it.
Where did India stand, and what did it secure?
India came to Antalya with a familiar brief. Story continues below this ad
While India remained dissatisfied with the dilution of the text on developed countries’ historical responsibility, it was successful in getting its key points into the draft text: a) developed countries’ Article 9.1 obligations were recalled; and b) equity and common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) were placed at the heart of implementation.

|

Interestingly, India also recognised the need for reducing anthropogenic methane emissions and the near-term climate benefits of reducing such short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs). This marks a welcome shift from its previous position, with India finally recognising the near-term climate benefits of reducing methane emissions while maintaining its stand on food security.
What does the lack of a unified vision mean for climate policy, and for India?
The easy reading is that Antalya failed. The harder one is that it failed honestly. A text that could not name fossil fuels, wrote a gigatonne aspiration for carbon capture into a UN decision and deleted the only number on adaptation finance would not have been a compromise. It would have been a step back dressed as consensus. No deal was better than that deal.
The cost of the stalemate is still real, and it falls on trust. The regime now runs on two currencies, ambition and money, and each camp holds one hostage to the other. Developed countries want fossil-fuel language without new finance. Producers want carbon capture without fossil-fuel language. Developing countries want finance before ambition. Under the consensus rule, everyone holds a veto and no one holds the pen.

The deeper risk is fragmentation. When parties to the UNFCCC cannot agree, rules get written elsewhere: in coalitions of the willing on fossil fuels, in voluntary pledges and in trade policy such as CBAM. These are spaces where CBDR carries little weight. For India, a weak multilateral process is not a win. It is the loss of the one forum where equity is the law of the room. The ICJ’s advisory opinion last year gave legal weight to arguments India has long made, but that weight is useful only in a forum that still works.
So, India must do two things at once. It must keep pressing for public finance and opposing unilateral trade measures at COP32 in Addis Ababa and through the second global stocktake that concludes in 2028. And it must move faster where no consensus text is needed: cutting methane emissions from waste and fossil fuels, phasing down HFCs under the Kigali Amendment, and reducing black carbon emissions. Cutting these super-pollutants is the quickest way to shave near-term warming. A summit without a deal is a setback. A decade without action would be a far bigger one.

title: The civilisational state: How the SCO forum reflects a shift in global politics
content_html:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi addresses the First Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum, in New Delhi on Friday. (DPR PMO/ANI Photo)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00
AI Translation

India hosted the inaugural Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi between November 20 and 22. The initiative reflects a growing trend in international relations to highlight civilisational identity and values as an effort to restore sanity and order in a strife-torn world.

The summit, proposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the SCO Summit in Tianjin in September 2025, aims to strengthen cultural ties and people-to-people exchanges among SCO countries. The forum comes even as geopolitical tensions, competing international orders and the weakening of multilateral institutions are reshaping global politics.

The idea of dialogue among civilisations is not new. At the 1893 Parliament of the World’s Religions in Chicago, Swami Vivekananda argued that world order and peace depend on mutual respect, assimilation, and universal acceptance, not on religious uniformity or cultural dominance. He presented Indian civilisational values, grounded in Vedantic unity, as an antidote to global sectarianism and materialism.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

In The Ideals of the East (1903), Japanese author Okakura Kakuzō argued that Asia shared a unified spiritual and cultural heritage, connecting Indian spiritual philosophy and Buddhism with Chinese thought and traditions. He saw Japan as a living repository that preserved and synthesised these continental ideals.

More recently, in 1988, Iranian President Mohammad Khatami proposed designating 2001 as the United Nations Year of Dialogue among Civilisations. This presented an alternative to Samuel Huntington’s clash of civilisations thesis, which argues cultural and religious identities drive the primary conflicts in the post-Cold War world.

Subsequent efforts include Kazakhstan’s Congress of Leaders of World and Traditional Religions (2003), the UN Alliance of Civilisations (2005), and Azerbaijan’s Baku Process (2008). India hosted the 2023 G20 summit with the theme Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (The world is one family). In 2024, the UN also established June 10 as the International Day for Dialogue among Civilisations.

First, what is a civilisational state?

American political scientist Lucian W. Pye introduced the term ‘civilisational state’ in his 1990 Foreign Affairs essay, China: Erratic State, Frustrated Society, to describe China’s distinctive historical and political character. He considered this difficult to understand within the conventional European nation-state framework. The concept subsequently attracted wider attention among scholars and commentators examining China’s historical continuity and international identity.

Story continues below this ad

A civilisational state can be understood as a sovereign nation whose identity is rooted in historical, religious, cultural and philosophical memories, traditions and practices. These extend well beyond its formation as a modern nation-state, linking its past with its present.

Also Read | With India as host, here are better goals for BRICS than ‘confronting the West’

Unlike the conventional nation-state, which focuses mainly on territorial sovereignty, citizenship and political institutions, the civilisational state draws on a longer historical inheritance to explain its identity, development choices and international role.

Over the last century, countries such as China, Russia, Turkey and India have progressed from promoting civilisational identity towards leveraging history, philosophical traditions and cultural ties as part of their foreign policy.

Why is the idea gaining importance?

The growing prominence of civilisational narratives is connected to the changing international order. The Russia–Ukraine war, US–China rivalry, conflicts in West Asia and declining confidence in multilateral institutions have encouraged countries to question the existing distribution of international power and influence.

Story continues below this ad

Emerging powers increasingly contend that Western political and institutional mechanisms should not be seen as universal models for international governance. Civilisational values provide an alternative framework for countries to coexist despite differences in religion, culture, economic circumstances, and political systems.

They also complement strategic autonomy: countries can maintain relationships with competing geopolitical powers without necessarily adopting their ideological or political systems. Rather than replacing conventional geopolitics, civilisational diplomacy adds a historical and cultural dimension in the pursuit of national interests.

How countries are using the idea

China: Challenging Western models of modernisation

China presents itself as a civilisation with thousands of years of historical continuity. Under Xi Jinping, this narrative has become important in explaining China’s developmental trajectory and international position. The Global Development Initiative (2021), Global Security Initiative (2022) and Global Civilisation Initiative (2023) illustrate this approach.

The Global Civilisation Initiative advocates respect for civilisational diversity, cultural exchanges and opposition to imposing one country’s values on others. Beijing’s argument is that modernisation does not need to follow a single Western pathway. This narrative also provides China with a diplomatic framework for engaging developing countries seeking greater autonomy in international affairs.

Russia: Positioning itself as a Eurasian civilisation

Story continues below this ad

Russia’s 2023 Foreign Policy Concept explicitly describes the country as a unique state-civilisation and a vast Eurasian and Euro-Pacific power. Moscow emphasises its Slavic, Orthodox Christian, European and Asian influences to distinguish its identity from Western political traditions.

China This Week | Trump, Xi and Putin’s declaration, Japan’s snub, and the Shenzhen story

This narrative supports Russia’s engagement with China, India and Central Asia and reinforces its advocacy of multipolarity through BRICS and the SCO. However, Russia’s claims to a broader historical and cultural space remain contested, particularly in Ukraine, where questions of sovereignty and independent national identity are central.

Turkey: Reviving Ottoman and Turkic connections

Under President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Turkey has given greater prominence to its Ottoman and Islamic heritage. Ankara uses historical and linguistic connections to strengthen relationships across the Middle East, Balkans and Central Asia.

The Organisation of Turkic States, connecting Turkey with Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, demonstrates how shared historical and linguistic identities can facilitate contemporary institutional cooperation.

Story continues below this ad

Civilisational identity also allows Turkey to expand its geopolitical engagement beyond its traditional European orientation.

The Western civilisational narrative

Civilisational politics is not exclusively a non-Western phenomenon. The second Trump administration’s 2025 National Security Strategy frames global politics around cultural and civilisational identity, warning of ‘civilisational erasure’ in Europe and positioning the US as a defender of Western cultural and religious heritage.

European debates surrounding Christian heritage, migration and cultural identity similarly demonstrate the growing importance of civilisational narratives in Western political discourse.

India: From civilisational heritage to engagement

India’s approach to civilisational diplomacy is distinctive because its historical experience encompasses multiple philosophical traditions, religions, languages and cultural exchanges. The government increasingly draws upon this heritage to establish India’s international identity.

Story continues below this ad

The 2023 G20 presidency theme, expressed through One Earth, One Family, One Future, presented an Indian philosophical principle as a framework for addressing shared global challenges. India’s efforts to secure permanent G20 membership for the African Union further reflected its emphasis on more representative global governance.

Three other dimensions are important.

First, Buddhism provides India with historical connections across Southeast and East Asia, Mongolia and Central Asia. Nalanda University, Buddhist diplomacy and cultural exchanges translate these historical connections into contemporary international engagement.

Second, India’s promotion of International Yoga Day demonstrates how traditional knowledge systems can acquire global recognition and become instruments of cultural diplomacy.

Third, civilisational identity reinforces India’s strategic autonomy. Its engagement with the US, Russia, Europe, China and the Global South shows that Indian foreign policy cannot be defined by membership in any particular geopolitical bloc.

Story continues below this ad

The SCO Civilizational Dialogue Forum extends this approach. By convening scholars, academics and cultural representatives, India seeks to broaden the organisation’s engagement beyond its traditional focus on security, economics and connectivity. Discussions of shared artistic traditions, architecture, manuscripts, languages and philosophical traditions highlight the historical interconnectedness of Eurasian societies.

For India, this also creates an opportunity to connect civilisational outreach with its wider Eurasian engagement, particularly with Central Asia and the South Caucasus.

Can civilisational diplomacy overcome geopolitical divisions?

Civilisational diplomacy can build cultural ties beyond conventional alliances, giving countries alternative ways to engage internationally through greater civil society participation and stronger people-to-people connections.

However, this also carries risks. Governments may selectively interpret history to strengthen domestic political legitimacy or claim cultural superiority. Historical ties may also be invoked to challenge neighbouring countries’ sovereignty and independent identities.

Story continues below this ad

India and China illustrate another limitation: shared Buddhist heritage has not prevented strategic rivalry and border tensions. Civilisational connections cannot substitute for political negotiations, economic cooperation or established international institutions.

The challenge is to ensure that civilisational identity becomes a source of dialogue rather than division.

Ultimately, the question is not which civilisation will dominate the international system, but whether distinct civilisational traditions can coexist and cooperate without hardening into rival geopolitical blocs.

For India, the opportunity is to turn its civilisational heritage into practical diplomatic partnerships while preserving its pluralistic traditions and strategic autonomy. The SCO Civilizational Dialogue Forum provides an important platform for this effort.

title: Rohingya genocide: Why the ICJ's verdict against Myanmar may never be enforced
content_html:
Rohingya women walking in an Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) camp in Rakhine state, Myanmar. (Wikimedia Commons)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

Written by Shashank Maheshwari

On November 19, the International Court of Justice found Myanmar had “committed genocide” against the Rohingya ethnic group in the country’s northern Rakhine province. This made Myanmar the first sovereign State to be held directly responsible for such a crime.

The judgment culminated a case initiated by Gambia against Myanmar in 2019. Just two years earlier, Myanmar’s army had carried out “clearance operations” against the Rohingya, and over 730,000 were displaced.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Both Gambia and Myanmar are parties to the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, under which every party is duty-bound to prevent genocide.

The court ordered Myanmar to pass genocide laws and prosecute those responsible, give guarantees against repetition, allow the safe return, restore property, search for the disappeared and provide medical care, and report within two years so that compensation can be decided. The court, however, refused to grant citizenship to the Rohingya.

While the judgment is significant, it remains to be seen whether Myanmar will obey it.

No effective enforcement mechanism

The court’s ruling was based on a rule in the International Law Commission’s (ILC) 2001 Articles on State Responsibility: the wrongdoer must undo the damage as far as possible.

Story continues below this ad

Article 1 creates responsibility for a wrongful act, which the State must stop under Article 30 and pay full reparation under Article 31.

These rules were built slowly and through compromise, even as the idea of holding countries responsible for violating international law has evolved.

Also in Explained | Why Myanmar’s genocide verdict matters, including for Israel’s case

In the early 20th century, powerful nations leveraged these rules against the countries they defeated, with Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles holding Germany and its allies responsible for the losses caused by World War I. International law scholar James Crawford described it as “a war indemnity disguised in legal language.”

An attempt to establish common rules failed at the 1930 Hague Conference because countries feared interference in their political decisions. It was only in 2001 that the ILC finalised the Articles on State Responsibility.

Story continues below this ad

However, objections from countries such as the United Kingdom led to the removal of a proposal to classify serious violations as crimes committed by States. Instead, Articles 40 and 41 required countries to cooperate to end certain serious violations and neither recognise nor support the resulting unlawful situations.

The UN General Assembly merely took note of these Articles in 2001 and deferred their adoption as a treaty in subsequent discussions in 2004, 2007 and 2010.

Thus, several provisions exist and reflect binding customary international law, but no party is assigned to enforce them. The Court admits as much: beyond the measures it ordered, “the choice of additional means must be left to Myanmar”.

The UNSC does not enforce ICJ judgments, even though it can

Story continues below this ad

The UN Charter provides a way to ensure that countries follow the ICJ’s judgments. Under Article 94(1), every UN member must comply with the Court’s judgments in cases involving that country. If a country refuses, Article 94(2) allows the other country involved in the case to approach the UN Security Council, which can recommend or take steps to enforce the judgment.

This provision was introduced when the UN Charter was drafted in 1945, after a proposal by China to grant the Security Council the power to enforce ICJ judgments.

However, the Security Council is not duty-bound to act, and any of its five permanent members can block substantive decisions through their veto power. As a result, even when the ICJ delivers a legally binding judgment, its enforcement can depend on political considerations rather than legal obligations alone.

In Nicaragua v. United States, the US lost a suit initiated by Nicaragua in 1984 over American support for the Contra rebels and mining of Nicaraguan waters. The US discontinued its participation in the case after it lost jurisdiction. In 1986, the court held that the US had broken international law and ordered it to stop and pay reparations, but the US ignored the ruling.

Story continues below this ad

When Nicaragua went to the Security Council, the US vetoed a draft resolution calling for full compliance on 28 October 1986. Nicaragua later withdrew its complaint after a change of government.

To date, the court has not enforced a judgment under Article 94(2).

Also Read | Why SC issued notice to Centre and CJI over appointments of judges

Myanmar, too, could evade enforcement by enlisting an ally’s veto power on the Council. A government that, in the Court’s words, still denies that the harm occurred, and which seized power during the case, is unlikely to write an honest restitution report.

How political compromise has shaped the definition of genocide

The history of international law reveals an uncomfortable truth: even the rules meant to prevent humanity’s worst crimes have been shaped by political interests. When Raphael Lemkin coined the word genocide in 1944, the idea went beyond mass killings. Early UN drafts also covered the destruction of a group’s culture.

Story continues below this ad

But the scope of the term was narrowed during negotiations over the 1948 Genocide Convention. Political groups that were initially included were later removed amid concerns that some countries would refuse to join. The definition also excludes cultural genocide, the systematic destruction of a group’s traditions, language, religion, heritage, and social identity.

As a result of this continued political compromise, the Genocide Convention protects only national, ethnic, racial and religious groups.

Nuremberg worked because the US, USSR, UK and France controlled Germany’s territory, government, and defendants. International law was enforced because these countries wanted it to be enforced.

However, subsequent examples have revealed that international law may be applied where the powerful find it convenient, and attacked, sanctioned, or ignored where they do not.

Story continues below this ad

When Israel captured Adolf Eichmann in Argentina in 1960, the UNSC, by eight votes to none, accepted that the transfer violated Argentina’s sovereignty, and asked Israel to make appropriate reparation. Within weeks, however, Argentina and Israel jointly declared the matter closed, and Eichmann was hanged in 1962.

The International Criminal Court’s 2024 arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu tells the same story. Neither the US nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute. The US responded with an executive order and sanctions on the ICC’s chief prosecutor and four ICC judges, while the US Secretary of State declared that Washington can take actions it deems necessary to protect the US, Israel, and other allies.

The present judgment is an official finding of genocide that grants courts and prosecutors an authoritative record, and supports other States’ duty not to treat the situation as lawful. But its enforcement still depends on whether powerful States choose to act. The ICJ can say what the law is. It cannot make a State follow it.

The author is an Assistant Professor at the Jindal Global Law School (JGLS) in Sonipat, Haryana.

Why Myanmar’s genocide verdict matters, including for Israel’s case
In the early 20th century, powerful nations leveraged these rules against the countries they defeated, with Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles holding Germany and its allies responsible for the losses caused by World War I. International law scholar James Crawford described it as “a war indemnity disguised in legal language.”
An attempt to establish common rules failed at the 1930 Hague Conference because countries feared interference in their political decisions. It was only in 2001 that the ILC finalised the Articles on State Responsibility.

However, objections from countries such as the United Kingdom led to the removal of a proposal to classify serious violations as crimes committed by States. Thus, several provisions exist and reflect binding customary international law, but no party is assigned to enforce them. The Court admits as much: beyond the measures it ordered, “the choice of additional means must be left to Myanmar”.
The UNSC does not enforce ICJ judgments, even though it can
Story continues below this ad
The UN Charter provides a way to ensure that countries follow the ICJ’s judgments. Under Article 94(1), every UN member must comply with the Court’s judgments in cases involving that country. If a country refuses, Article 94(2) allows the other country involved in the case to approach the UN Security Council, which can recommend or take steps to enforce the judgment.
This provision was introduced when the UN Charter was drafted in 1945, after a proposal by China to grant the Security Council the power to enforce ICJ judgments.
However, the Security Council is not duty-bound to act, and any of its five permanent members can block substantive decisions through their veto power. As a result, even when the ICJ delivers a legally binding judgment, its enforcement can depend on political considerations rather than legal obligations alone.
In
Nicaragua v. United States

The US discontinued its participation in the case after it lost jurisdiction. In 1986, the court held that the US had broken international law and ordered it to stop and pay reparations, but the US ignored the ruling.
Story continues below this ad
When Nicaragua went to the Security Council, the US vetoed a draft resolution calling for full compliance on 28 October 1986. Nicaragua later withdrew its complaint after a change of government.
To date, the court has not enforced a judgment under Article 94(2).

Myanmar, too, could evade enforcement by enlisting an ally’s veto power on the Council. A government that, in the Court’s words, still denies that the harm occurred, and which seized power during the case, is unlikely to write an honest restitution report.
How political compromise has shaped the definition of genocide
The history of international law reveals an uncomfortable truth: even the rules meant to prevent humanity’s worst crimes have been shaped by political interests. When Raphael Lemkin coined the word genocide in 1944, the idea went beyond mass killings. Early UN drafts also covered the destruction of a group’s culture.
Story continues below this ad
But the scope of the term was narrowed during negotiations over the 1948 Genocide Convention. Political groups that were initially included were later removed amid concerns that some countries would refuse to join. The definition also excludes cultural genocide, the systematic destruction of a group’s traditions, language, religion, heritage, and social identity.
As a result of this continued political compromise, the Genocide Convention protects only national, ethnic, racial and religious groups.
Nuremberg worked because the US, USSR, UK and France controlled Germany’s territory, government, and defendants. International law was enforced because these countries wanted it to be enforced.
However, subsequent examples have revealed that international law may be applied where the powerful find it convenient, and attacked, sanctioned, or ignored where they do not.
Story continues below this ad
When Israel captured Adolf Eichmann in Argentina in 1960, the UNSC, by eight votes to none, accepted that the transfer violated Argentina’s sovereignty, and asked Israel to make appropriate reparation. Within weeks, however, Argentina and Israel jointly declared the matter closed, and Eichmann was hanged in 1962.

The International Criminal Court’s 2024 arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu tells the same story. Neither the US nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute. The US responded with an executive order and sanctions on the ICC’s chief prosecutor and four ICC judges, while the US Secretary of State declared that Washington can take actions it deems necessary to protect the US, Israel, and other allies.
The present judgment is an official finding of genocide that grants courts and prosecutors an authoritative record, and supports other States’ duty not to treat the situation as lawful. But its enforcement still depends on whether powerful States choose to act. The ICJ can say what the law is. It cannot make a State follow it.

title: Adani’s Tarali project: The dispute over its cost and wildlife fee
content_html:
The 1,500-megawatt Tarali PSP is proposed on the Tarali dam reservoir and spans 150.74 hectares of non-forest land in Nivade, Tondoshi, Kalambe and Jalu villages in Patan taluka of Satara district. (File)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The Maharashtra Pollution Control Board (MPCB), in a letter to Adani Green Energy Ltd, has directed it to stop excavation and construction work linked to its Tarali hydropower project in Satara district.

It said the “excavation/development work” at Sawarghar village was done without permission from the MPCB and without obtaining environmental clearance. The company has said these are construction-support facilities and do not form part of the permanent project components, which “have the requisite statutory clearances”.

This comes amid the controversy over Adani Green’s affidavit regarding the cost of the 1,500 MW Pumped Storage Project (PSP), proposed on the Tarali dam reservoir.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

The Indian Express reported that the renewable energy company ow­ned by the Adani Group had sought to sharply revise the declared cost of its 1,500 MW hydropower project to Rs 56.75 crore from Rs 5,675 crore. This revision proportionally reduced the amount the company was required to deposit towards wildlife conservation and protection to Rs 2.27 crore, from Rs 227 crore.

The project spans 150.74 hectares of non-forest land in Nivade, Tondoshi, Kalambe and Jalu villages in Patan taluka of Maharashtra’s Satara district.

Here’s what to know about the project cost revision, the wildlife conservation deposit, and the questions it has raised.

Why was Adani Green Energy asked to deposit Rs 227 crore?

Story continues below this ad

A letter issued by the Union Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC) on February 11, 2025, recommending the grant of prior Environment Clearance to the Tarali PSP, mentioned the project cost as Rs 5,675 crore.

According to the state forest department, the project falls within the deemed Eco-Sensitive Zone (ESZ) of the Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary in Satara, which is part of the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve (STR). A senior forest officer told The Indian Express that, under existing norms, private companies setting up projects in an ESZ can be asked to deposit up to 4% of the project cost towards conservation and protection.

Also Read | Adani slashes Maharashtra power project cost by 99%, its forest dues plummet; Centre orders probe

Accordingly, at its meeting on February 23, 2026, the State Board for Wildlife (SBWL) laid down 15 conditions for the project. One of these required 4% of the project cost to be deposited in the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve’s bank account.

In a letter to Adani Green Energy dated March 24, 2026, Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife) M Shrinivas Reddy listed the 15 conditions laid down by the SBWL and asked the company to deposit Rs 227 crore — 4% of the project cost of Rs 5,675 crore — into the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve Conservation Foundation. Reddy also asked the company to submit an affidavit confirming that it would fulfil the 14 other conditions. The project proposal would then be forwarded to the National Board for Wildlife (NBWL) for consideration.

Story continues below this ad

In another letter to Adani Green Energy, dated May 7, 2026, the Deputy Director of Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary said: “Cost of the project passing through the buffer/deemed eco-sensitive zone of Koyna Wildlife Sanctuary is Rs 5,675 crores and its 4% amounting to Rs 227 crores should be deposited in the bank account of Field Director of STR”.

How did the calculation change to Rs 2.27 crore?

On September 8, 2026, Adani Green Energy’s Chief Operating Officer Naresh Telgu submitted a notarised affidavit regarding the project cost to the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (PCCF), Maharashtra.

The affidavit stated: “While submitting the part IV the cost of the project is considered based on analogous estimation, we considered as INR 56.75 crore, request you to please consider the same as project cost.”

Also Read | Adani project stopped after Rs 227 crore wildlife fee cut to Rs 2.27 crore

On October 12, PCCF Reddy informed Adani Green Energy that his office had accepted the revised project cost of Rs 56.75 crore. He asked the company to immediately deposit 1% of this amount (Rs 56.75 lakh) and pay the remaining 3% (Rs 1.7075 crore) after the NBWL’s approval. The company subsequently deposited Rs 56.75 lakh into the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve’s bank account.

Story continues below this ad

On October 30, Rohan Bhate, Honorary Wildlife Warden of Satara district, registered a complaint on the Prime Minister’s grievance redressal portal and the Maharashtra government’s Aaple Sarkar grievance redressal portal, alleging an “incorrect cost of the project”. On November 6, the MoEF&CC directed the state forest department to investigate the matter on priority. The state forest department has initiated a probe.

What did the company say?

In its first response, an Adani Group spokesperson had said: “All the Tarali PSP elements are within private land ownership across three revenue villages in Patan taluka and have no Forest land. PSPs do not have any adverse impact on the downstream ecology, environment, forest, or wildlife in the area during operations.”

After The Indian Express published its report on November 13, the company issued a statement rejecting the allegation that it had sought to revise the project cost downwards to reduce its statutory obligations.

Also Read | Maharashtra Pollution Control Board stops work at Adani project

The spokesperson said: “The allegation that the company sought to revise project costs downwards to diminish statutory obligations is completely misleading. The online proposal in the Forest/wildlife portal was solely for site investigation purposes, while SBWL considered total project costs of Rs 5,675 crore. Since site investigation costs are around 1% of project costs, therefore clarification of the project Rs 56.75 crore representing solely the site investigations and survey costs, for the online proposal was provided.”

Story continues below this ad

The spokesperson added: “Secondly, the allegation that downward revision was intended to lower conservation costs is false. The Tarali PSP is situated entirely on private, non-forest land and 3.2 kms away from the Koyna wildlife sanctuary. It is outside the notified buffer zone of Sahyadri Tiger reserve and in no way impacts or fringes upon the tiger corridor or any notified Eco Sensitive zone. The project does not cause diversion of any protected areas, any reserve forest or notified Eco Sensitive zone.”

Why did the forest department halt project work?

On November 13, within hours of The Indian Express report, the forest department ordered all work at the Tarali PSP site to stop immediately. The department said work had commenced without prior approval from the NBWL, which it considered mandatory because the project site falls within the deemed ESZ of the Sahyadri Tiger Reserve.

The forest department sought a detailed written explanation from the company, asking it to clarify under what authority and on what basis it had commenced work without NBWL approval. The company was also asked to submit all statutory clearance documents and maps related to the Tarali PSP, along with copies of permissions from the competent authority for cutting trees at the project site.

Responding to the order, Adani Green Energy said in a statement: “No component of the Tarali Pumped Storage Project falls within any notified Protected Area and no forest land is involved in the project. Further, necessary permissions/NOCs relating to land use and statutory requirements have already been obtained from the competent authorities.”

Story continues below this ad

The company also said it had secured Environmental Clearance on February 11, 2025, and Consent to Establish on April 7, 2025, after which construction began. It said wildlife clearance proceedings had been initiated, and that its proposal was pending consideration by the NBWL.

title: From Steve Jobs to Jensen Huang, the unending cult of the American tech founder
content_html:
(From left) Steve Jobs, Sam Altman, Jensen Huang. (Wikimedia Commons, file)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00
AI Translation

Eleven days after he stepped down from Nvidia amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Jensen Huang has returned as the chief executive of the artificial intelligence (AI) chipmaker.

His reinstatement, following the intervention of US President Donald Trump and mounting pressure from investors, marks one of the most dramatic corporate comebacks in recent Silicon Valley history.

While the circumstances surrounding Huang’s departure and subsequent return are unusual, American technology companies have a long history of turning to their founders in times of crisis. From Apple’s Steve Jobs to OpenAI’s Sam Altman, some of the industry’s most prominent executives have returned to lead the companies they helped build, in some instances after being unceremoniously ousted by their boards.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

Also Read | What Jensen Huang’s return means for Nvidia and the AI ecosystem

These comebacks also reflect the peculiar relationship that Silicon Valley has with its founders, whose individual personalities, technological vision and ability to command investor confidence can become almost inseparable from the companies they run.

The success of executives such as Jobs has helped perpetuate the belief in Silicon Valley that founders possess an intuitive understanding of their businesses that professional managers cannot easily replicate. However, Huang’s comeback presents a somewhat different proposition. Unlike Jobs, who returned to an Apple facing business challenges, Huang’s reinstatement followed a crisis precipitated by revelations about his own conduct.

His return, even as investigations remain underway, also raises questions about the extent to which the commercial indispensability of a founder can supersede conventional considerations of corporate governance and accountability. There are many unanswered questions around national security, governance and political intervention surrounding Huang’s reinstatement too.

Story continues below this ad

Here is a look at some of Silicon Valley’s most high-profile founder comebacks, the circumstances that led to their return, and how they shaped the fortunes of their companies.

Steve Jobs, Apple (1997)

Arguably the most famous corporate comeback in Silicon Valley’s history is that of Steve Jobs, who co-founded Apple in 1976 with Steve Wozniak.

In 1985, following a bitter power struggle with then Apple CEO John Sculley, whom Jobs himself had recruited from PepsiCo, the company’s board sided with Sculley, leading to Jobs’ departure. He went on to establish computer company NeXT and subsequently acquired the business that became animation studio Pixar.

Steve Jobs with the Macintosh computer in January 1984. He would be fired the next year. (Wikimedia Commons)

By the mid-1990s, Apple was struggling financially and losing ground to Microsoft-powered personal computers. Its acquisition of NeXT brought Jobs back into the company, and in September 1997, he became its interim CEO.

Story continues below this ad

What followed was one of the most remarkable turnarounds in corporate history. Under Jobs, Apple launched the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad — products that fundamentally altered the consumer technology industry. By the time Jobs stepped down in August 2011, Apple had become one of the world’s most valuable companies, and continues to.

Sam Altman, OpenAI (2023)

Perhaps the closest parallel to Huang’s dramatic reinstatement is the return of Sam Altman as OpenAI’s CEO in November 2023 – sans the numerous extramarital affairs.

OpenAI’s board abruptly fired Altman in November 2023, saying that he had not been consistently forthcoming in his communications with directors. The decision came barely a year after the launch of ChatGPT, which had catapulted OpenAI to the forefront of the global AI industry.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. (Wikimedia Commons)

The sacking triggered a revolt within the company, with an overwhelming majority of its employees threatening to leave unless Altman was reinstated. Microsoft, OpenAI’s biggest financial backer at the time, offered to hire Altman and his colleagues.

Story continues below this ad

Also Read | Why is Sarvam AI offering Chinese AI models, and what does it mean for India’s AI ambitions?

Within days, an agreement was reached for Altman’s return, accompanied by an overhaul of OpenAI’s board. An independent review subsequently concluded that his conduct did not warrant his removal.

The episode demonstrated how even a board specifically constituted to prioritise the safe development of AI could find itself at odds with the commercial interests of investors and employees.

Michael Dell, Dell (2007)

Michael Dell, who founded his eponymous computer company in 1984, while retaining the position of chairman. His successor, Kevin Rollins, struggled with intensifying competition and slowing growth, prompting Dell’s return as CEO in January 2007.

Story continues below this ad
Michael Dell stepped down as Dell CEO in 2004 but returned in 2007. (Wikimedia Commons)

In 2013, Dell took the company private in a $24.9-billion deal with private equity firm Silver Lake, allowing it to undertake a restructuring away from the scrutiny of public markets.

Three years later, the company acquired data storage giant EMC in a landmark technology deal, transforming Dell from a business largely associated with personal computers into a major enterprise technology and computing infrastructure company.

Jack Dorsey, Twitter (2015)

Jack Dorsey, Twitter’s co-founder and first CEO, was pushed out of the position in 2008 amid concerns over his management of the fledgling social media platform.

Jack Dorsey returned as Twitter CEO in 2015. (Wikimedia Commons)

In 2015, as Twitter struggled to expand its user base and faced pressure from investors, Dorsey returned as CEO following Dick Costolo’s resignation. For the next six years, he simultaneously ran Twitter and payments company Square.

Story continues below this ad

When Dorsey stepped down again in November 2021, handing over the reins to India-born Parag Agrawal, he explicitly questioned the culture of founder-led technology companies, arguing that excessive dependence on founders could become a limitation for businesses.

Larry Page, Google (2011)

Google co-founder Larry Page relinquished the CEO position in 2001 to Eric Schmidt, an experienced technology executive brought in to manage the rapidly expanding company.

In 2015, Larry Page oversaw Google’s corporate restructuring under a new parent company, Alphabet. (Wikimedia Commons)

A decade later, Page reclaimed the position, with Schmidt becoming executive chairman. Unlike several other high-profile founder comebacks, the transition was not precipitated by an acrimonious boardroom battle.

In 2015, Page oversaw Google’s corporate restructuring under a new parent company, Alphabet, allowing its core Internet business and more experimental technological ventures to operate separately. He became Alphabet’s CEO, while Sundar Pichai took charge of Google.

Google co-founder Larry Page relinquished the CEO position in 2001 to Eric Schmidt, an experienced technology executive brought in to manage the rapidly expanding company.

title: AI stocks rebound: How Nvidia’s comeback lifted Asian and US markets
content_html:
A dealer walks near the screens showing the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) and the foreign exchange rate between U.S. dollar and South Korean won at a dealing room of Hana Bank, Friday, November 20. (AP)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00
AI Translation

Asian and American stock markets were in a lull in November amid anxiety that the AI (artificial intelligence) bubble could pop. That was until Jensen Huang’s comeback into the top job at Nvidia, which lifted these AI-driven markets to their best day in months.

After a sharp crash following Huang’s resignation earlier in the month, the US’ clean chit on the Chinese spy controversy and his comeback to Nvidia led to the chipmaker regaining nearly a third of its value, lifting other AI-led markets in the process.

Lull period for AI-led markets

The US markets have had a poor month so far, dropping as much as 11% until the sharp gains on Monday. The AI-related fears have pulled down the share prices of big names like Google’s parent company Alphabet, the newly-listed Anthropic, and Meta, among others.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

These AI fears deepened after Huang, a top name in the AI space, exited the company, and after Democrats’ thumping win in the mid-term elections sparked concerns about a slowdown in AI spending.

Also Read | In Jensen Huang’s return, unanswered questions of national security, governance and politics

The rut had been far deeper for Asian markets that are largely driven by AI. After reaching record highs amid AI optimism earlier this year, the South Korean, Japanese, and Taiwanese markets had fallen sharply from their peaks till Monday. The South Korean Kospi index had lost nearly half its value. The Japanese and Taiwanese indices had lost 20-30%.

While the US had some of the biggest names in the AI and tech space, Asian markets like Taiwan and South Korea are largely driven by AI stocks. For example, chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix hold almost half the weightage on the Kospi, while TSMC alone accounts for 40% of Taiwan’s benchmark index.

Huang’s return lifts sentiment

Nvidia’s board announced Huang’s return late on Monday, days after ruling out any such possibilities. US President Donald Trump also expressed support for this decision, giving Huang a clean chit on his extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Story continues below this ad

His reinstatement lifted shares of Nvidia, which had crashed over 40% since his extramarital affair allegations first surfaced in late October, by 31.5% – the biggest single-day gain since 2003. Other AI players like Meta, Alphabet, and Oracle shot up by 6-12%. This lifted the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite index by 6.5%, helping Wall Street recover from the 8% selloff last week.

Also Read | From Steve Jobs to Jensen Huang, the unending cult of the American tech founder

“Nvidia is the biggest and most important name in AI, and the whole industry is dependent on their chips. And Nvidia and Huang are synonymous. So his comeback is a big positive for the industry in terms of stability and direction,” a head of research at a domestic broking firm said.

Major firms like Morgan Stanley and Bernstein, which had downgraded their view on Nvidia after Huang’s exit, calling it a “big setback”, also started to reverse their opinion after his comeback. Bernstein, for example, upgraded their rating on the stock on Monday, just days after downgrading it post Huang’s resignation.

The comeback also sparked a rally across Asia. The Kospi jumped 7% early on Tuesday. Taiwan’s Taiex index skyrocketed 9%. Japan’s Nikkei 225 also gained 4%. While the Indian markets are shut on the occasion of Prakash Gurpurb Sri Guru Nanak Dev, the GIFT Nifty was up 0.4%, signalling that the benchmark Nifty 50 and Sensex may open on a positive note on Wednesday.

title: What the Ayodhya-Janakpur train says about India’s railway diplomacy
content_html:
The decorated Saryu-Kamala Express inaugural special train at the Ayodhya Junction on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. (Photo: PTI)
AI Narration
Listen
00:00

The Prime Ministers of India and Nepal, Narendra Modi and Balendra Shah, Monday flagged off the first passenger train between the two countries from Ayodhya to Janakpur. Named Sarayu-Kamala Express, the train will cover a distance of over 600 km in around 19 hours and will have stops at Gorakhpur, Basti, Raxaul, Sitamarhi, Madhubani, and Jaynagar.

The move will not only strengthen cross-border connectivity and diplomacy between the two countries, but it also provides a link between two significant religious sites for Hindus — Ayodhya (for Ram) and Janakpur (for Sita).

The project is also part of India Railways’ ambitious Ramayana, Buddhist and Shiv-Shakti circuits by linking Janakpur-Ayodhya, Lumbini-Bodhgaya-Sarnath-Kushinagar and Kathmandu (Pashupatinath)-Varanasi.

Story continues below. Subscribe to see fewer ads.

“In 2025 alone, around 30 crore pilgrims from across the country and the world visited Ayodhya. With the launch of the Saryu-Kamala Express train service today, we are adding a new dimension to this sacred bond. This will now make it easier for pilgrims visiting Ayodhya to travel to Janakpur to seek blessings of Mata Sita,” said PM Modi in his address.

He further said that India will work together to enhance connectivity between sacred sites in both countries.

Key projects

India and Nepal share religious, cultural and historical ties. The movement of people between the two countries has remained uninterrupted over the years, with people from either side frequently crossing the border for jobs, tourism, marriages, etc. The Railways have now undertaken several projects traversing these regions to facilitate the seamless cross-border movement of people.

Jaynagar-Bijalpura-Bardibas and Jogbani-Biratnagar are two important ongoing railway projects between India and Nepal. Apart from this, the Raxaul-Kathmandu railway line is another ambitious cross-border project.

Story continues below this ad

Along with the flagging of the express train, the two leaders announced the finalisation of the Field Location Survey for the proposed Raxaul-Kathmandu electrified broad-gauge railway line, and announced that the two sides will collaborate in the development of the East-West Railway in Nepal.

“Apart from these projects, as part of capacity building, Nepal Railway officers and staff have been imparted training on various aspects related to train operations at Gatishakti Vishwavidyalaya, Vadodara,” said a senior Railway official.

Other cross-border projects

Nepal is not the only neighbouring country where Indian Railways is looking to extend its network. Last year in September, the government announced two cross-border railway projects to connect Bhutan with the bordering areas of Assam and West Bengal. The 69-km Kokrajhar (Assam)-Gelephu (Bhutan) and 20-km Banarhat (West Bengal)-Samtse (Bhutan) lines will cost Rs 3,456 crore and Rs 577 crore, respectively.

Currently, the Himalayan nation Bhutan does not have a railway network. It was the result of almost two decades of efforts made by India and Bhutan to formally announce the two strategic projects.

Story continues below this ad

Earlier, India operated cross-border trains Maitree Express and Bandhan Express to Bangladesh, which was suspended in July 2024 following the unrest in the neighbouring country. Bandhan Express used to run between Kolkata (India) and Khulna (Bangaldesh) and Maitree Express between Kolkata to Dhaka Cantonment.

Indian Railways earlier also operated the famous Samjhauta Express and Thar Express between India and Pakistan. Both trains were suspended in August 2019 due to sustained tension between both countries after the government revoked the special status of Jammu & Kashmir.

India has also planned a rail link to Myanmar. The Jiribam-Imphal section (125 Km), which falls within Indian territory, is under construction. The remaining portion from Imphal to Moreh in India is yet to take off and the section from Tamu to Kalay (128) in Myanmar has not been sanctioned.
